title: Whatever you ask
hook: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives (Dhanasri M5, ang 681)
tomorrow: As the Word comes to me, Lalo

segments.voice: Yesterday, one father: we are all children of the One, with no membership test. Today the week closes with a bold promise about asking.

A kid with a request runs the numbers fast: one parent for the late curfew, the other for the money, a grandparent for the extra dessert. Asking is a skill. You learn who will say yes, how to phrase it, when to wait. Then, in Raag Dhanasri, comes a line from Guru Arjan that seems to skip all that strategy: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives. No angles. No timing. It sounds almost too simple. So what is it saying?
screen: `WHICH PARENT TO ASK.` → `ASKING IS A SKILL.` → `WHATEVER YOU ASK, HE GIVES.`

segments.voice: The line is on ang 681: jo maageh thaakur apune te, soee soee devai. Whatever is asked of one's own Master, that very thing He gives. It continues, in effect: whatever the servant Nanak speaks, it comes true, here and hereafter. Thaakur is master, lord, the one you belong to. Notice the small word apune, your own: not a distant ruler you petition through officials, but your own Master, the one who already knows you. Now, the honest question. Does this mean a person gets anything they want? The hymn gives the context. The one speaking is the daas, the servant: Nanak calls himself that in the very next line. One reading is that a servant who lives close to the Master starts to want what the Master wants. Elsewhere Gurbani speaks of bhaana, the Will, and of asking first for the Name. So the line is less a blank check than a picture of trust between a servant and a good master: the servant isn't afraid to ask, and the Master doesn't hold back. Some Sikhs also say, from experience, that what's given is sometimes not what was asked, but what was needed: strength instead of escape, patience instead of speed. Look back at the week. Partners, all. Pitaa. Mihar. Kaudi: not for a shell. Hargobind, a gift arriving. One father, all his children. And now thaakur: a week about belonging, and about asking like someone who belongs.
screen: `THAAKUR: YOUR OWN MASTER.` · `THE SERVANT WHO ASKS IN TRUST.` · `NOT A BLANK CHECK: THE WILL.` · `THIS WEEK: BELONGING, THEN ASKING.` · then, large: `ASK YOUR MASTER.`

segments.voice: Let your wants come up, the big and the petty, without judging them, then let them settle and see which one is truly good, for you and for others: courage, maybe, or healing for someone, or patience with a child. If you pray, you can ask the One for it simply, the way a child asks a parent they trust; if you don't, hold it as a hope.
Thaakur, master, lord, the one you belong to: Guru Arjan says whatever is asked of your own thaakur, He gives; the trust of a servant who belongs.
Your line: ask your master. Trust, not a blank check. A week of belonging, complete.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Dhanasri shabad in kirtan and often recall its line 'jo maageh thaakur apune te soee soee devai' when making an Ardas, alongside acceptance of the Will.

fork.setup: you've read: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives. what do you ask for?
options: one truly good thing, in trust.
nothing; it's too good to be true.
fork.reveal: the line is spoken by a servant, the daas, who trusts the Master enough to ask plainly.

original.note: Gurmukhi: master, lord; jo maageh thaakur apune te, whatever is asked of one's own Master.

trapdoor: what you thought: pray and you'll get what you want.
what it means: a servant who belongs can ask without fear, and the Master gives.
what a scholar hears: the promise is framed by the daas relationship and by Gurbani's wider teaching on bhaana and asking for naam; read alone, it is often misheard as transactional.

chat.says: Does that hymn mean God gives you anything you ask for?
options: Less a blank check than trust: sometimes what's given is what was needed instead.
Yes, any wish at all, as long as you phrase the request just right.
No, asking is wrong; a Sikh should never ask for anything at all.
chat.meaning: The speaker is the daas, the servant; the line is less a blank check than a picture of trust between a servant and a good master.
